cells.tense: Right now the practice and the exchange are both lit, and neither one is eating the other.
cells.ask: Offer one thing today without tracking what comes back.
cells.core:
You do the work quietly — the repetition, the small refinements — and you let what you hand over move through people without keeping the ledger open on it. That's harder than it sounds. Most people who give well are still counting, and most people who practice well are doing it for themselves alone.
The two feed each other here. The practice makes you steady enough to give without flinching, and the exchange keeps the practice from becoming a locked room. This stretch is one where those two aren't in conflict. Some weeks the quiet part will pull harder, and some months the return won't match what you put in. What holds is that you keep the small light lit and keep handing something over. Today, offer one thing and don't note down what comes back.
cells.sheetLine: You give and you practice, and neither one is costing you the other.
cells.verb: Giving and receiving in even measure
cells.place: A small practice kept lit by daily attention

cells.tense: You're already at the next exchange in your head, bracing for the return before you've given anything.
cells.ask: Make one exchange this week where you don't decide the outcome first.
cells.core:
You hand something over, and before it lands you've already worked out the terms — what comes back, what you'll say if it doesn't, how to adjust if it comes up short. Something in you is doing that arithmetic all day. But the practice has turned into pre-negotiating every trade, and the other person can feel the terms underneath the gesture.
Fairness doesn't need that much planning. It needs you to hand something over and wait. What you're bracing against is a return that hasn't happened yet and might not look the way you've scripted it. The hours you've put into refining what you do — that's what steadies you when the return is slower or stranger than expected. This week, make one exchange and don't script the ending. Let it come back or not come back, and stay in the room either way.
cells.sheetLine: You're scripting the trade before you've made it.

cells.tense: The practice sits behind you, and you're not showing anyone what you're working on.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you're actually working on this week.
cells.core:
You still do what's asked of you. What's gone quiet is the small repetitive thing that used to be yours alone — and you're not saying what you're practicing to anyone, which means nobody can give anything back into it. The quiet isn't peaceful anymore; it's just empty of exchange.
Forcing yourself to give more won't help. You can't push feeling into a room that's gone still. What you can do is sharpen what you're already paying attention to — notice one thing clearly, make one distinction, and let one person in on it. That's not grand. It's the smallest unit of exchange. Say what you're working on to someone, badly if it comes out badly, and let them respond. The practice comes back when it has somewhere to go.

cells.tense: The exchange is already happening through you, and you haven't claimed it as something you're doing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you handed over this week as yours, not as something that needed doing.
cells.core:
Needs get met around you, and you move toward them before anyone asks. You've done this long enough that it feels like the natural order — as if the exchange happens around you rather than because of you. It's running. What's missing is your name on it.
What you call practical is actually a discipline. You've refined it — you notice faster, you hand things over cleaner, you let things come back more easily than you used to. That took repetition. But it arrives unclaimed, and the person doing it hears no acknowledgment from the one person who should know. Not because thanks are owed. Because something you don't claim is something you can't decide to keep or change. This week, name one thing you handed over as yours.

attempts.check: The draw doesn't say the person has made giving and receiving a practice in the ways I'm describing in the Too Much and Too Little cells — the record gives me the seat and the status, not their history. A reader could reasonably say 'I give plenty and it drains me, that's not a discipline problem.' The ask survives being wrong because it asks for one concrete exchange, not for a diagnosis to be right — anyone can try it and learn something either way. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about what fairness is 'really' underneath the surface.
